clue.text: The apparent promise starting a famous book

definitions.text: The apparent promise starting a famous book

parts.words: The apparent promise starting a famous book
parts.note: the opening words of Genesis, first book of the Bible, which also sound like a hopeful first move, as if things were promising at the outset

explanation.surface: A celebrated volume opens with what looks like a pledge.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bible opens with these three words; the 'apparent promise' is the idea that a beginning holds promise of what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis opens with this phrase, the most famous start of any book in English.

clue.text: Surprisingly honest cup scores

indicators.note: surprisingly suggests the letters of the two words come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A remarkably upright trophy keeps the tally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surprisingly' signals a rearrangement of HONESTCUP.
explanation.definitionFit: To notch up is to score or achieve, as in a tally cut in wood.

clue.text: Australian writer's high points

definitions.meaning: belonging to Ernestine Hill, the Australian author and journalist

explanation.definitionFit: Ernestine Hill was an Australian writer, and hills are elevated ground.

clue.text: Gardener's verge by the side of the new bare ground

indicators.note: by the side of places one piece directly next to the other
ground is the past tense of grind, so the words are crushed into a new order

parts.note: a verge is a rod or staff of office carried in ceremonies

explanation.surface: A gardener's lawn edge lies beside freshly cleared earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' turns THENEWBARE into BENWEATHER; the gardener is Ben Weatherstaff in Frances Hodgson Burnett's The Secret Garden. 'Verge' looks like a grass edge but is the ceremonial rod.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Weatherstaff is the old gardener at Misselthwaite Manor in The Secret Garden.

clue.text: In economics, Margery rejected a Marxist

indicators.note: rejected means the hidden run is thrown back and read in the other direction
In shows the letters sit inside the words economics and Margery

explanation.surface: In an economics class, Margery turned down a communist.
explanation.walkthrough: The run ICSMARG lies inside 'economics, Margery'; 'rejected' turns it round. Antonio Gramsci was an Italian Marxist thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio Gramsci was an Italian Marxist philosopher and founder of the Italian Communist Party.

clue.text: MulloverFrench townandsecure over-fiftymurdersuspect

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'MulloverFrench townandsecure over-fiftymurdersuspect' with spaces lost; NESS (Mull) around VILLE, LAND and L accounts for all but one E, and no clue word plainly gives it.

clue.text: A good way to quote words written by trendy politician

parts.note: trendy things are in, fashionable
Con is short for a Conservative politician
the words written down form a text

explanation.surface: A fashionable MP's written remarks are best quoted with care.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces run in answer order: IN, CON, TEXT. 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Quoting with the surrounding passage preserved keeps the original meaning, which is fair quotation.

clue.text: Famous actress with a costume Oscar

parts.note: garb is clothing or costume
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A screen star wins an Academy Award for costume design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' looks like the film award but is the radio code word for O.
explanation.definitionFit: Greta Garbo was a celebrated Swedish-born Hollywood film star.

clue.text: She killed many men in Catalan tales

indicators.note: in tells us the name lies within the words Catalan tales

explanation.surface: Catalan folklore tells of a woman who slew many men.
explanation.walkthrough: Atalanta raced her suitors and had those who lost put to death.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth, the huntress Atalanta had suitors who lost a footrace to her executed.

clue.text: Ministers having sex withescorts?

parts.note: sex is Latin for six, VI in Roman numerals
Escorts were Ford cars

explanation.surface: Clergymen accused of sleeping with paid companions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sex' is Latin for six (VI); the Ford Escort was a popular car, so escorts are CARS.
explanation.definitionFit: Vicars are parish clergy, ministers of the Church.

clue.text: What I've just mentioned is a 1970s USpoetry journal

definitions.meaning: a pointer word for something just referred to
an American little magazine of poetry founded in the 1970s

explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun refers back to something just said, and the US poetry magazine of that name began in 1971.

clue.text: Large penny pulled out from body of water in Europe, Birmingham, or an African city

annotationWithheld.why: Held as 'Large penny pulled out from body of water in Europe, Birmingham, or an African city'; no body of water losing L and P (or D) gives the answer, and no search found the intended parse.
annotationWithheld.clue: Large penny pulled out from body of water in Europe, Birmingham, or an African city

clue.text: Sex with feeling welcomed by once single Bond girl

indicators.note: welcomed by means the first pieces are taken in by the later word

parts.note: sole is an archaic word for single or unmarried
it is slang for sex appeal
air is a feeling or atmosphere

explanation.surface: An erotic feeling is received by a formerly unmarried Bond girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' marks the archaic sense of single. Solitaire is the tarot-reading heroine of Live and Let Die; 'Sex' leads the surface but is only IT, sex appeal.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitaire is the psychic heroine of Fleming's Live and Let Die, one of the 007 women.

clue.text: Hartley's emotional manipulator perverted valet with dope

indicators.note: perverted means twisted out of shape, so the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A manservant drugged and corrupted plays on feelings in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perverted' rearranges VALET and DOPE. The Love-Adept is a novel by L P Hartley.
explanation.definitionFit: L. P. Hartley's novel The Love-Adept centres on a figure skilled at manipulating affections.

clue.text: Almost cancel long-lasting spells

indicators.note: almost means the word falls just short, its final letter dropped

parts.note: to erase is to cancel or wipe out

explanation.surface: Nearly calling off enduring periods of magic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spells' looks like magic but means periods of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Eras are long historical periods, extended stretches of time.

clue.text: Weapon in a two-part Shogun reading

parts.note: split the word Shogun into two parts, SHO and GUN, read as show and gun; show is air, gun is pistol

explanation.surface: A weapon appears in a two-volume reading of a samurai epic.
explanation.walkthrough: Shogun is James Clavell's novel; split and read as 'show gun', it gives AIR (to air is to show) and PISTOL (a gun).
explanation.definitionFit: An air pistol is a handgun that fires pellets using compressed gas.

clue.text: Celebs rejectedthis dodgy dealer

indicators.note: rejected means the word is thrown back and read the other way

parts.note: celebrities are VIPs, very important persons

explanation.surface: Famous people spurned a shady trader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns VIPS round. A spiv is British slang for a flashy small-time crook trading in black-market goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiv is a petty black-market trader, a flashy wheeler-dealer.

clue.text: Generations following some children's fiction

definitions.meaning: for all time afterwards, through the generations to come
fairy tales, which close with the formula about living happily for the rest of time

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means for all subsequent time, and ends the stock fairy-tale closing line.

clue.text: "He rides for days on just a pony for a friend" (Oklahoma!)

definitions.text: "He rides for days on just a pony for a friend" (Oklahoma!)

parts.words: "He rides for days on just a pony for a friend" (Oklahoma!)
parts.note: a line from The Farmer and the Cowman with two words cut out after 'on'; the song runs 'for days on ... just a pony'

explanation.surface: A lyric about a lonely cowboy from a Rodgers and Hammerstein musical.
explanation.walkthrough: The song's line is 'He rides for days on end, with just a pony for a friend'; the missing words fill the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The two words dropped from the cowboy lyric complete the phrase 'days on end' and lead into 'with just a pony'.

clue.text: Made contact with Lincoln in news publication finally printed

parts.note: a broadside is a sheet printed on one side, used for news and ballads

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word printed

explanation.surface: A newspaper finally printed a story about Abraham Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lincoln' suggests the president, but here it is a Lincoln car struck side-on.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadside is to hit a vehicle side-on, so a Lincoln car was struck.

clue.text: Loot — an abridgement of an Ionesco play

indicators.note: an abridgement shortens the title, cutting its tail away

parts.note: Rhinoceros is the absurdist play by Eugene Ionesco

explanation.surface: Stolen goods, and a shortened version of an absurdist drama.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhino is old British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhino is old slang for money or cash, much like loot.

clue.text: One visiting revolutionary writer Kiley

indicators.note: visiting means one piece goes to stay inside the other

parts.note: a revolutionary is a red, a communist
one is I in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A revolutionary author is paid a call by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary writer' looks like John Reed, but the writer is the American novelist Kiley Reid, author of Such a Fun Age.
explanation.definitionFit: Kiley Reid is the American novelist who wrote Such a Fun Age.

clue.text: Beer with no head rejected as visibly old-fashioned

indicators.note: rejected means the shortened word is thrown back and read the other way
with no head means the first letter is removed

parts.note: porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: Beer without froth is sent back as obviously outdated.
explanation.walkthrough: PORTER loses its head to give ORTER, which 'rejected' turns into RETRO. 'head' suggests froth on a pint.
explanation.definitionFit: Retro styling deliberately imitates past fashions, looking dated by design.

clue.text: Biblical general is protected by backing wargod

indicators.note: protected by means the word is sheltered inside the other piece
backing means the god's name runs backwards

parts.note: Ares is the Greek god of war

explanation.surface: An Old Testament commander is shielded by a war deity in retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns ARES into SERA before 'protected by' wraps it around the second piece. Sisera appears in Judges 4.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisera was the Canaanite commander killed by Jael in the Book of Judges.

clue.text: A kind of equality in a Milan Kundera novel

definitions.meaning: in mathematics, an equation true for every value of its variables
Kundera's 1998 novel about a couple's sense of selfhood

explanation.definitionFit: In algebra an identity is an equation holding for all values; Kundera also wrote a novel with that title.

clue.text: Swift creation that's superb or not as good as some others?

definitions.text: Swift creation that's superb or not as good as some others?

parts.words: Swift creation that's superb or not as good as some others?
parts.note: Swift's imaginary lands lie beyond the real globe; the phrase also means excellent, and is teased as if it meant falling short of other worlds

explanation.surface: Is Jonathan Swift's invention brilliant, or does it trail its rivals?
explanation.walkthrough: Gulliver's Travels takes readers to fantasy lands; the phrase means superb, but the question mark plays on it as if 'out of' meant excluded from a ranking.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means wonderful, and Lilliput and Laputa are lands beyond the real earth.
